population.note: FICTIONAL. Adoption has plateaued: 11.5% of ~265M adults ≈ 30.5M current users. Cycling arithmetic: 18.0 ever − 11.5 current = 6.5% of adults who used and are off now; ~40% of current users are restarters (≈4.6% of adults) and ≈1.4% of adults are off again after at least one restart, so cycled = (4.6 + 1.4) / 18 ≈ 33% of ever-users. That fits the parent's ~35% one-year persistence and 36–47% restart rate. The age mix is shifting even though the total barely moved. 65+ rose from 9 to 10.5% because the Medicare Bridge was extended. 50–64 eased from 22 to 20% as employer coverage kept eroding. Under-30 use is flat to falling (≈5%), partly the aesthetic inversion among young urban adults. Age-weighted check: 0.20×5 + 0.33×10 + 0.24×20 + 0.23×10.5 ≈ 11.5. Payer split of the ~30.5M: employer/commercial ≈14M, Medicare Part D diabetes ≈5M, Medicare Bridge obesity ≈2.1M, Medicaid (14 states at $245) ≈1.2M, cash/TrumpRx/direct ≈8M; total ≈30.3M. Never-users who would qualify by BMI are ~60M adults. They are concentrated in the bottom income third, the uninsured and states without Medicaid coverage. Pediatric: ~0.4% of under-18s, mostly adolescents 12+, still skewed to upper-income families. Under-12 use stays off-label under specialist care. Several million children now grow up in households where an adult eats roughly a third less.

access.public_coverage: Medicare GLP-1 Bridge was extended by CMS in Nov 2027 on identical terms through Dec 2029: Medicare pays $245/month, beneficiary copay $50, same BMI/comorbidity criteria. That is an extension, not a statutory benefit. Arithmetic: ≈2.1M obesity enrollees × $245 × 12 ≈ $6.2B/year gross. This runs above the CBO pace (≥$35B over 2026–2034 ≈ $3.9B/yr average) and is a live budget complaint. Medicaid: 14 states adopted coverage at the $245 rate, ≈1.2M enrollees × $245 × 12 ≈ $3.5B/year combined federal+state. The rest of the states decline. AUD use is reimbursed case by case under medical necessity, not as a covered benefit.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generics remain at roughly $8–48/month, and generic oral semaglutide is now launching in India. Canada and Brazil have multiple generics (Canada ~CAD 70–110/month). Generic semaglutide is available in ~160 countries. US exclusivity is unchanged (~2031–32).
access.note: Managed decline: TrumpRx and direct channels list oral Wegovy and Foundayo at $129–149 for starter doses and $199 at maintenance. Injectable Zepbound/Wegovy vials and pens run $249–299 cash. Wegovy list stays nominally $1,349, and nobody pays it. Oral share of new starts reached ~45% in 2028 (≈20% in 2026). The shift came after the 2027 head-to-head result: CVS Caremark and Express Scripts moved to 'oral-first' step therapy for new starts. Injectables hold the high-efficacy tier (tirzepatide, retatrutide). Employer coverage drifted from 60% to 56%, with no structural change. Among covering employers GLP-1s are ~12% of claims. The FDA finalised the 503B exclusion in early 2027. Compounding is a residual niche. Personal importation of Indian generics is a known but small channel; FDA occasionally seizes mail shipments.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Dec 2026)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved May 2028)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: alcohol use disorder: guideline-endorsed (APA/ASAM joint update, Apr 2027) as a conditional second-line option for AUD in adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes. VA formulary added it. No FDA AUD label yet; Novo's oral semaglutide AUD phase 3 is enrolling
mainstream_offlabel_uses: alcohol reduction in adults without obesity, citing the 2027 guideline beyond its stated population
'quiet' / 'food noise' low-dose use by people without obesity via cash telehealth, marketed as calm and focus
nicotine and gambling craving reduction, still observational
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: Oral parity was realised within the approval rules through an existing product in a new form. The OASIS-H2H trial (Jun 2027) showed oral semaglutide 25 mg non-inferior to injectable Wegovy 2.4 mg at 68 weeks (15.1% vs 15.8%). The FDA added comparative data to the label in Sep 2027, and orforglipron's top dose sits in the same band. No pill matches tirzepatide or retatrutide. The efficacy frontier moved back to a needle when retatrutide was approved in May 2028, 15 months after its Feb 2027 BLA. Its label carries dysesthesia and a 'consider dose reduction for reduced pleasure' line. CagriSema was approved in Dec 2026 against placebo but trades as a second-line brand after REDEFINE-4. Amycretin phase 3 continues, with filing expected 2029. Survodutide was filed Mar 2028, so no decision before 2029. MariTide monthly injectable and bimagrumab muscle adjuncts are still in trials and not on the US market. Global incretin revenue was ~$105B in 2027, with growth slowing per unit as prices fall.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common effect and the leading cause of discontinuation. Orals show similar GI rates to injectables at matched efficacy.
Elevated with rapid weight loss; more visible with retatrutide's larger losses.
Low absolute risk; no causal confirmation in longer follow-up.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; multidistrict litigation ongoing, no verdicts.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ~25–40% of lost weight is lean mass, varying with exercise and protein intake. Concern intensified with the 28% retatrutide losses and older Bridge enrollees.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change; ADA/Obesity Society guidance (2027) recommends resistance training and protein targets for adults 65+.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Additional cohorts remain split; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label stands; FDA added it to postmarketing adverse reactions section (2027) without a boxed or class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal; anhedonia findings were explicitly analysed separately from suicidality.

FDA's Oct 2027 class labelling drew on pooled reanalysis of trials that added the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale after 2026, plus a Sentinel cohort. It estimates clinically meaningful reduced pleasure in ~5% of users vs ~2% on placebo, dose-dependent and usually reversible within 4–8 weeks of dose reduction or stopping. Across ~30.5M users the ~3-point excess implies roughly 0.9M people affected at any time.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class label (Adverse Reactions + Patient Information): 'reduced interest or pleasure in activities; consider dose reduction'. No boxed warning. The label's own wording became marketing vocabulary.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Trial and real-world figures still diverge (one-half to two-thirds regained at a year in most analyses). Cycling makes it the population's typical experience.
Further observational signals (iron, B12, vitamin D) in long-term users eating ~30% less.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; professional guidance suggests periodic labs.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; adolescents on decades-long therapy; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Now ~6 years of rigorous follow-up for semaglutide; nothing for adolescents beyond ~4 years; no cycling data designed to detect harm.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on retatrutide and CagriSema; NIH-funded cycling cohort launched 2028.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: New reports fell sharply after the 503B exclusion. Residual cases come from imported and counterfeit product.
Reported in phase 3 at single-digit percentages, mostly mild.

food_and_beverage.state: Volume pressure persists but has stopped accelerating, because adoption plateaued. Snack and confectionery units are down low single digits annually. Protein and 'small-format' lines are now standard. A counter-trend has appeared: 'unapologetic' full-size and full-fat premium lines aimed at young urban never-users, led by a few craft snack and dairy brands. Big CPG now runs two portfolios aimed at two appetites.

alcohol.state: Contraction deepened after the AUD guideline. Heavy drinkers, the top 10% who carry ~60% of sales, are now a clinical target population. Spirits volumes are down mid-single digits since 2026, and distributors report the steepest loss in high-volume value tiers. Premium 'occasion' pours and non-alcoholic lines hold up; no category offsets the loss.

restaurants.state: Traffic is steady and the menu has split. Chains push small plates and protein bowls. In New York, Chicago and Los Angeles a visible niche of 'appetite' restaurants (large shared plates, long tasting menus, no half portions) markets itself to the unmedicated. It is small in revenue but loud in press.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep shrinking and closing stores. Straight-size churn has normalised. Athletic and 'built' fits (broader shoulders, roomier thighs) grow, driven by the muscle ideal among 18–34s.

fitness.state: Strength gyms and hybrid strength studios are growing, on two engines: muscle preservation for older on-drug users (now in ADA guidance) and the muscle-as-status ideal among younger never-users. Cardio-only boutiques decline.

insurance.state: No structural change. Employer coverage drifted to 56%, pill-first step therapy cut per-member cost, and retatrutide is behind prior authorisation almost everywhere. Payers are watching AUD diagnosis codes rise on GLP-1 claims and have begun audits.

pharma.state: Still essentially a Lilly–Novo duopoly in the US, with Lilly ahead on retatrutide and Foundayo and Novo leaning on the oral Wegovy parity result. Revenue still grows, but net price per patient has fallen ~30–40% since 2026 through negotiated channels. Growth now comes from new indications (AUD trials) and the high-efficacy tier rather than new users.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Among affluent adults over 40, a lean body still reads as 'on it' and is unremarkable. Among college-educated 22–34s in coastal metros (Brooklyn, Silver Lake, Austin's east side), leanness now reads as medicated and slightly dated. Visible muscle and a big appetite eaten in public read as 'natty', a word borrowed from bodybuilding meaning unmedicated.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Thinness has gotten cheaper ($129–299 cash, $8–48 abroad) and therefore less distinguishing. The new scarce ideal costs time rather than money: trained muscle, cooking, eating heavily without gaining. The bottom income third is the least medicated and the least able to buy the new ideal, so it is shut out on both counts.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: GLP-1 households eat smaller and more scheduled meals, and 'food noise' is ordinary vocabulary. Among younger urban never-users the shared feast is back as a status event: dinner parties judged by how much is eaten, and 'second dinner' on menus.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: In LA and New York, 'natty' and 'never on it' are common self-written dating-app bio tags. Since the 2027 label, partners openly ask whether a flat mood is 'the dose'. Some couples renegotiate dosing around anniversaries and holidays. Teenage girls in upper-income suburbs treat 'never been on it' as a quiet boast; teen boys' muscle-focused protein culture intensifies, and pediatricians report more muscle-dysmorphia concern.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has split in meaning. For the medicated majority of the middle-aged it is a signal to manage. For a young urban minority it is proof of vitality, something to display. Craving of all kinds is now openly clinical territory since alcohol entered the guidelines.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Labelled Oct 2027: clinically meaningful reduced pleasure in ~5% of users vs ~2% on placebo, dose-dependent and reversible. That is ≈0.9M excess cases among ~30.5M users. Milder 'quieting' that falls below clinical thresholds is reported by many more users and is exactly what is being sold.
interior_life.framing: Simultaneously a labelled adverse effect, a guideline-endorsed treatment (for AUD) and a lifestyle benefit. Cash telehealth brands sell the sub-threshold version as 'quiet': freedom from craving, steadier focus, calm. Manufacturers stay inside 'food noise' language. Clinicians call the clinical version anhedonia. Users mostly say 'turned down'.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Sales, trading and startup cultures discuss 'quiet' openly as a focus aid, and some founders post about dosing for deep-work weeks. Employers neither encourage nor police it, and HR guidance treats it as private medical information. No productivity studies exist; anecdotes run both ways (less distraction, less ambition).
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Musicians and comedians talk about the dose on stage. A minor genre of 'natty' open mics and gigs in Brooklyn and Chicago bills itself as unmedicated. Some writers describe dose holidays to finish work. Sour, spicy and extreme-flavour products keep growing among users seeking reward. Some amateur athletes in run clubs report losing the post-race high.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Reduced desire and connection are now a recognised, nameable reason for couples' therapy referrals. The label gave partners a script. Dose-reduction-for-intimacy is a common clinical conversation.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Rhetorical, not electoral. The administration touts $149 pills via TrumpRx, while the MAHA wing of the same coalition celebrates 'unmedicated vitality' and attacks 'quiet' marketing, an open intra-coalition friction. A widely shared academic preprint found no turnout difference by GLP-1 use. Online, 'are they dosed?' has become a sneer at calm politicians.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access on price and approvals: retatrutide approved on schedule, comparative oral label granted. The compounding crackdown is complete. FDA has sent a handful of untitled letters to telehealth firms over 'quiet' marketing but has not acted structurally; there was no new state action this step.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Price-controlled access unchanged in structure: Medicare Bridge extended at $245/$50, Medicaid optional at $245 (14 states), TrumpRx cash at $129–299.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Coverage still conditioned on BMI/comorbidity and prior authorisation. Payers audit AUD-coded GLP-1 claims for diagnosis drift. There is no adherence monitoring beyond standard refill data.
state.workforce_or_military: None. The military retains standard waiver rules for recruits on GLP-1s; no programme exists.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The US–India price gap (≈$199 vs ≈$20/month) remains a standing political talking point, and India's generic oral launch sharpened it. Manufacturers continue trading price concessions for tariff relief. Supply is no longer constrained.

still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US; exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32.
Medicare's GLP-1 Bridge terms are unchanged: Medicare pays ~$245/month and the beneficiary copay is ~$50, with the same BMI/comorbidity criteria.
Indian generic semaglutide still sells at roughly $8–48/month across dozens of brands.
Wegovy's US list price remains nominally $1,349/month, and almost nobody pays it.
Only roughly a third of weight-management starters remain on therapy at one year, and a large minority of stoppers restart within a year.

events.event: APA and ASAM publish a joint AUD guideline update endorsing semaglutide as a conditional second-line option for adults with alcohol use disorder and obesity or type 2 diabetes; VA adds it to formulary for that use

Novo's OASIS-H2H trial finds oral semaglutide 25 mg non-inferior to injectable Wegovy (15.1% vs 15.8% at 68 weeks); CVS Caremark and Express Scripts move to oral-first step therapy for new obesity starts
FDA adds 'reduced interest or pleasure' to class labelling for GLP-1-based obesity drugs, citing ~5% incidence vs ~2% placebo, dose-dependent and reversible; no boxed warning
CMS extends the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge demonstration through December 2029 on unchanged $245/$50 terms; Medicaid uptake stalls at 14 states

Cash-pay telehealth firm Stillwater Health passes 1.1M members on its $179/month 'Quiet' oral plan, advertised as 'turn down the noise'; FDA issues untitled letters over focus and calm claims but the plan stays live
FDA approves Lilly's retatrutide (28% mean weight loss) as a weekly injectable with dysesthesia labelling; it launches behind prior authorisation at most payers

open_tensions: The same labelled effect is a warning, a guideline-endorsed AUD treatment and a $179/month wellness product. Payers are already auditing AUD codes, and nobody has decided whether 'quiet' for people without obesity is medicine.
Pills reached injectable parity just as the efficacy frontier moved back to a needle (retatrutide, 28%). Coverage rationing now sorts people by tier, not by route.

The aesthetic inversion makes unmedicated muscle the young urban ideal while the uninsured bottom third can afford neither drug nor the time-costly ideal. Medicare's Bridge is running above the CBO pace on a demonstration, not a law.
A third of ever-users have cycled, children are growing up in households that eat a third less, and the first cycling cohort has only just been funded.

prose.headline: The Pill Got as Good as the Needle. The Label Now Says It Can Dull Your Joy. 1.1 Million People Are Paying for That Part.
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 the incretin drugs have stopped spreading and become part of the furniture. About one American adult in nine is on one, roughly where things stood two years ago. Nearly one in five has tried one. A third of those who tried have already stopped and started again at least once. The growth story is over. What is left is a settled population, and the questions are about who is in it and what it feels like to be in it.

The pill made the difference in kind. A head-to-head trial in mid-2027 showed oral semaglutide doing what the weekly Wegovy injection does. The two big pharmacy benefit managers made the pill the default for new patients, and close to half of new starts now never see a needle. The needle has not disappeared, though. Lilly's retatrutide was approved in May and takes off more than a quarter of body weight. It is a weekly shot, and almost every insurer keeps it behind prior authorisation. Patients are now sorted less by pill versus shot and more by tier: the cheap, adequate pill, or the expensive, dramatic injection.

Prices have come down without breaking. Through TrumpRx and the manufacturers' own direct channels a month of pills costs $129 to $199 and a pen up to about $299. India sells the same molecule for the price of lunch. Wegovy's list price is still $1,349, a number that now mostly sits on a pharmacy screen. Employers keep edging away, and only 56 percent still cover weight management. Medicare's Bridge pilot was meant to end in 2027. It was extended on the same $245 terms and costs about six billion dollars a year, faster than the Congressional Budget Office projected. Fourteen state Medicaid programmes joined. The rest did not, so the people least likely to be on the drug are still poor, uninsured and living in those states.

The interesting change is inside people's heads. In October 2027 the FDA added a line to every label in the class: reduced interest or pleasure in activities, in about five percent of users against two on placebo, dose-dependent and reversible. Six months earlier the psychiatric and addiction societies had endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in people with obesity. The same quieting of the brain's reward system is now, formally, a side effect and a treatment at once. A third reading came from the market. Stillwater Health, a cash telehealth company, sells a $179 a month 'Quiet' plan to more than a million members, advertised as turning down the noise. The FDA has sent letters. The plan is still running. In sales offices and startups people talk about dosing for focus the way an earlier generation talked about Adderall, with less shame and less adrenaline.

The culture is turning away from thinness itself. Among college-educated twenty-somethings in Brooklyn and Silver Lake, a lean body has come to look medicated, slightly middle-aged, bought. The new marks of status cost time rather than money: visible muscle, a big appetite eaten in public, the bodybuilder's word 'natty' written into a dating profile. Restaurants in New York and Chicago advertise portions that will not be halved. Strength gyms are growing, filled at 6 a.m. by retirees told to protect their muscle and at 7 p.m. by their grandchildren chasing a look. Spirits makers are watching their heaviest drinkers drift away, this time on prescription. The administration boasts about the pill price while its own wellness wing jeers at people who have had their cravings quieted. None of it looks like a crisis. It looks like a country that has quietly split its appetites in two.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marisol Reyes takes the pill at 6:10 a.m. with four ounces of water, standing at the sink in Columbus, and then waits thirty minutes before coffee because the label says to. Her dental group dropped weight coverage in January. Now it's $199 a month through TrumpRx on her own card, and the reminder lands on the second.

At the office she eats half a turkey wrap at eleven and forgets the other half until four. Dr. Kessler's hygienist is back on Zepbound and talks about it as if it were the weather.

At lunch her daughter Ana texts from Brooklyn: a photo of a table crowded with bread, a whole fish and three pastas. Caption: second dinner lol. Ana has never taken it. She says she never will. She lifts four mornings a week, and Marisol thinks her shoulders look like her father's.

On the drive home Marisol puts on the Juan Gabriel album she played at her wedding. She waits for the part where her throat used to close up. It's pleasant. It is a pleasant song.

She made the dosage call last month, when Ray asked again whether she was 'in there.' The nurse practitioner said they could drop her to the lower dose and see. She hasn't decided. Two pounds came back in March, the first time in a year.

Ray grills. She eats one chicken thigh and a lot of the tomatoes, and he watches her eat in a way he thinks she doesn't notice.

At ten she reads the patient leaflet again, the new paragraph near the bottom. Reduced interest or pleasure. Consider speaking with your doctor. She folds it back along its old creases.
